solution: Preemptive scheduling of n jobs on m identical machines with release times and deadlines, which is feasible iff a transportation-style flow saturates. Cut the timeline at the sorted distinct r_i and d_i values (at most 400 boundaries, so <= 399 intervals) and build source -> job i (cap p_i) -> interval k (cap len_k, present only when [t_k,t_k+1) lies inside [r_i,d_i]) -> sink (cap m*len_k); a schedule exists iff max flow equals sum p_i, because any schedule induces such a flow and any flow can be realised. Realise it with McNaughton's wrap-around inside each interval: lay the per-job amounts end to end along a strip of length m*len_k and cut it into m printer rows, which never splits a job across two rows at the same instant since each amount is <= len_k. Dinic on ~600 nodes and ~80000 edges per dataset.
statement_summary: Up to 200 files, each with a page count, a release time and a deadline, must be printed on m identical printers; printing may be interrupted and resumed on any printer, but a file may occupy only one printer at a time and each printer prints one page at a time. The task is to decide feasibility and, when feasible, emit an explicit schedule.
notes: Both samples match (YES with a valid schedule / NO). The interval-compressed flow agrees with a flow built over individual unit time slots on 360 random instances, and with an exhaustive slot-by-slot DFS on the 300 tiny ones; every schedule produced was re-validated against all the statement's rules (per-file totals, windows, no self-overlap, no printer overlap). The statement's output constraint is misprinted as d_i <= x < y <= r_i; it must mean r_i <= x < y <= d_i.
